title: Family Problem Solving
subtitle: Some drift is not a slip to correct but a signal that a small system is wrong, and quick fixes will never settle it, because you keep patching the symptom while the cause sits untouched. audience: Readers who have finished five of the six S's, taken on the keeping mindset (a home is kept and not finished, on small shared habits) with Chapter 26, and started the friendly check-in with Chapter 27. Busy home keepers and parents. Their check-in keeps surfacing the same stubborn problems, the same coats on the same chair, the same dishes by the sink, week after week, and they want a way to settle those for good instead of patching them forever. They do not need Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, or Standardize re-taught, nor the audit from Chapter 27 re-taught (this chapter USES its findings), nor the daily-times system (Chapter 29) or the recurring 6S event (Chapter 30) built here; they need the shared method for solving the recurring problems the audit turns up, and above all the blameless spirit that makes it work. The danger for this audience is two-fold: the chapter can read as a cold corporate problem-solving framework, or as a tense, blaming family meeting; it must be neither, but light, human, genuinely shared, children included, and above all blameless. Nobody is ever the problem; a recurring problem is a design flaw, not a character flaw. The emotional heart is relief, the relief of stopping an exhausting cycle of patching the same thing forever.

the_reframe_and_the_method.fixing_is_not_solving: The core distinction. Fixing and solving are two genuinely different activities, and we confuse them constantly, to our exhaustion. Fixing is correcting the symptom, the coats are on the chair so you hang them up, and it is necessary, quick, and completely temporary, because it does nothing about whatever put the coats there, which is still fully in place and will do it again tonight. Solving looks past the symptom to the cause and changes that, so the symptom stops being produced; fixing is mopping the floor, solving is finding the leak, and if you find yourself mopping the same square of floor every single day, some part of you already knows that more mopping is not the answer, and the recurring problems your check-in keeps surfacing are that same square of floor. The fixing-versus-solving reframe, frozen: a problem you have to fix more than twice is not a problem you are failing to fix, it is a problem you are failing to solve, fixing puts the thing back, solving changes why it fell in the first place, so that you never have to put it back again. The definition box, frozen: family problem solving is how a household settles the recurring problems a home throws up, together, when the same thing keeps drifting back, you stop patching the symptom, ask why it keeps happening rather than who is to blame, and change the small system so it cannot easily happen again, it fixes the cause once, instead of the symptom forever.
the_reframe_and_the_method.ask_why_not_who: The method's heart, extending the audit's no-blame spirit. The tool for finding the cause hinges entirely on asking the right question, because the wrong question sends you in exactly the wrong direction. Ask who keeps dumping their coat on the chair and you get a defensive family member, a small argument, and a coat that is back tomorrow, because you have identified a culprit but changed nothing about the situation that produced the behaviour; ask why the coats keep landing on the chair and you are looking at the real thing, the chair right by the door, the hooks down the hall, and every tired person doing the sensible, path-of-least-resistance thing. Nobody is failing; the system is simply asking people to walk further than a tired human will walk. You get from symptom to cause by gently asking why a few times, the way a curious child would, and you notice something reassuring, the real cause is almost always a design flaw, not a character flaw, a missing hook, an awkward distance, a bin too far, a shelf with no label, a thing with no home, which is genuinely good news, because you cannot easily change a person, but you can nearly always change a system. The why-not-who reframe, frozen: when something keeps going wrong, the useless question is who keeps doing it, and the useful one is why it keeps happening, who finds a person to blame and changes nothing, why finds a system to fix and changes everything, the coats are not on the chair because someone is lazy, they are on the chair because the hooks are in the wrong place.
the_reframe_and_the_method.solve_it_together: The ownership move. What decides whether a solution survives is not how clever it is, but who came up with it; you met this principle when you assigned the standards a few chapters back, what is chosen gets done and what is imposed gets subverted, and it is doubly true for problem-solving, for two reasons. The first is knowledge: the person who actually lives with the problem knows things about why it happens that you, solving it from the outside, simply do not, so leave them out and you will design a worse solution. The second is ownership: any fix, however good, needs the people around it to keep using it, and people keep what they helped build and abandon what was dropped on them from above. So you bring the recurring problem to the household, out loud, as a shared puzzle rather than a verdict, and you let everyone, including the children, who are often startlingly good at this, propose the fix; the solution you land on together will be better than the one you would have imposed, and, far more importantly, it will still be running in a month. The solve-together reframe, frozen: the person who lives with a problem is the one who knows why it really happens, and the one who has to keep any fix alive, so they are exactly who should help design it, a solution handed down is resented and quietly dropped, a solution the household worked out together is one it actually keeps.
the_reframe_and_the_method.the_four_step_method: The method in action, on the coats. The method is just four small steps, done together. First, name the problem plainly, as a problem and not a person, the coats keep ending up on the chair. Second, ask why, together, a few times, and arrive not at a guilty party but at a cause everyone recognizes the moment it is said, the hooks are down the hall, the chair is right there, and tired people take the shortest path. Third, change the small system to remove that cause, a row of hooks goes up on the wall right beside the door, so now the shortest path and the right path are the same path. And fourth, because the whole family worked it out and one of the kids picked where the hooks went and got to hammer one in, it is theirs, and they use it, so the problem that returned every week for a year quietly stops returning at all, and it works on almost anything, the dishes, the shoes, the homework, the endless small recurring frictions of a shared home. The four-step method, frozen: solve a recurring problem together in four small steps, name the problem that keeps drifting back, ask why, a few times, until you reach the real cause, change the small system so the cause is gone, and let the people who live with it help decide the fix, so they keep it.

definition: Family problem solving is how a household settles the recurring problems a home throws up, together: when the same thing keeps drifting back, you stop patching the symptom, ask why it keeps happening rather than who is to blame, and change the small system so it cannot easily happen again. It fixes the cause once, instead of the symptom forever.
rule: When the same problem keeps coming back, stop fixing it and start solving it: ask why it happens, not who is to blame, and change the system so it cannot easily happen again.
four_step_method: Solve a recurring problem together in four small steps: name the problem that keeps drifting back; ask why, a few times, until you reach the real cause; change the small system so the cause is gone; and let the people who live with it help decide the fix, so they keep it.
fixing_versus_solving_reframe: A problem you have to fix more than twice is not a problem you are failing to fix. It is a problem you are failing to solve. Fixing puts the thing back; solving changes why it fell in the first place, so that you never have to put it back again.
why_not_who_reframe: When something keeps going wrong, the useless question is who keeps doing it, and the useful one is why it keeps happening. Who finds a person to blame and changes nothing; why finds a system to fix and changes everything. The coats are not on the chair because someone is lazy. They are on the chair because the hooks are in the wrong place.
solve_together_reframe: The person who lives with a problem is the one who knows why it really happens, and the one who has to keep any fix alive, so they are exactly who should help design it. A solution handed down is resented and quietly dropped; a solution the household worked out together is one it actually keeps.

callouts.quick_win: Take the one thing in your home you are tired of fixing, the pile that always returns to the same spot, and ask out loud, "why does this keep happening here?", three or four times, until you reach something you can actually change. You just started solving it instead of fixing it.
callouts.family_challenge: Bring one recurring annoyance to the whole household, phrase it as "why does this keep happening?" and never "who keeps doing this?", and let everyone, including the children, propose a fix. The best solution often comes from the very person you were about to blame.
callouts.sixs_tip: The real cause is almost always a design flaw, not a character flaw: the bin is too far, the hook is too high, the shelf has no label, the thing has no home. When a problem keeps returning, look for the missing or awkward part of the system before you look at the people.
callouts.common_mistake: Solving the problem for the family instead of with them, by imposing a clever fix nobody asked for. However good it is, it will be resented and abandoned within a fortnight, because people keep what they helped build and drop what was dropped on them. Solve it together, or do not bother.
